title: Two Stages of Folding: Convergent Mechanisms in AI Protein Folding Trunks
claim: Across different architectures, patching sequence representations works in early blocks while patching pairwise representations works in later blocks, showing a shared two-stage organization.
layout: 3 side-by-side area plots under a left-to-right structure strip; shared legend below
description: The top strip shows a left-to-right progression of protein structures. A gray unfolded chain leads, via an orange arrow, to a blue and red hairpin. A orange-to-green gradient arrow then leads to a green hairpin, and a green arrow leads to a gray folded hairpin. Below the strip are three area plots, one each for ESMFold, OpenFold and Boltz-1. The x-axis is block index (0 to about 48). The y-axis is the percent of outputs with the donor motif (0 to about 40). In each plot an orange-tan area for sequence patches is high at the earliest blocks and falls to zero. A gray-green area for pairwise patches rises in later blocks and peaks around blocks 35 to 40. In Boltz-1 the green area is nonzero from the start. A shared legend at the bottom labels Stage 1 (sequence patch) and Stage 2 (pairwise patch). The eye goes first to the orange spikes on the left of each plot, then to the green peaks.
caption: Two computational stages in AI protein folding trunks. We identify which latent representations in ESMFold, OpenFold, and Boltz-1 influence secondary structure formation by patching activations from a hairpin protein into a helical protein at each block of the trunk, then measuring whether the output folds as a hairpin (or vice versa). Sequence patches (orange) induce hairpin formation in early blocks; pairwise patches (green) are effective in later blocks.
abstract: How do protein structure prediction models fold proteins? We investigate this question through causal interventions on the folding trunks of ESMFold, OpenFold, and Boltz-1. Across all three models, we find a shared two-stage computational structure. In the first stage, early blocks initialize pairwise biochemical signals: features like charge propagate from sequence into pairwise representations through architecture-specific pathways. In the second stage, late blocks develop pairwise spatial features: distance and contact information accumulate in the pairwise representation. We verify these mechanisms causally by showing that steering charge and distance features induces predictable structural changes. Furthermore, these representations are functionally interchangeable: pairwise states can be linearly aligned and substituted across models. Together, these results suggest that folding trunks with different architectures, inputs, and training procedures converge on a shared representational organization for mapping sequence chemistry into spatial geometry.
